The Crane: a past life story (Ja 38 1.1)

The clever cheat cannot achieve
ultimate happiness by cheating.
The clever cheat succeeds only
in getting what the crane did from the crab.
Nanda: a past life story (Ja 39 1.1)

I suspect the heap of gold
and golden chains
is where the house-born slave Nandaka
stands yelling curses.
The Pit of Acacia Coals: a past life story (Ja 40 1.1)

Fine, let me fall
head over heels into hell,
but I shall not do what is ignoble.
Please accept my alms offering.
About Losaka: a past life story (Ja 41 1.1)

One who does not follow advice when instructed
by an ally who desires their good,
grieves like Mittaka
hanging off a goat’s foot.
The Pigeon: a past life story (Ja 42 1.1)

One who does not follow advice when instructed
by an ally who wants to help,
not following the pigeon’s counsel,
ends up in the hands of their foes.
The Pole Acrobat: a past life story (Ja 43 1.1)

One who does not follow advice when instructed
by an ally who wants to help,
ends up destroyed
like the pole acrobat’s father.
The Mosquito: a past life story (Ja 44 1.1)

Better is a considerate foe
than an inconsiderate friend.
Thinking, “I shall kill the mosquito”,
the idiot son split open his father’s head.
About Rohinī: a past life story (Ja 45 1.1)

Better is an intelligent foe
than a foolish sympathizer.
See that wretched Rohinī,
grieving after killing her mother.
Spoiling the Park: a past life story (Ja 46 1.1)

Surely not with one who misunderstands the meaning
does good conduct lead to happiness.
The simpleton destroys the good,
like the monkey groundskeeper.
Spoiling the Toddy: a past life story (Ja 47 1.1)

Surely not with one who misunderstands the meaning
does good conduct lead to happiness.
The simpleton destroys the good,
as Koṇḍañña did the toddy.
About Vedabbha: a past life story (Ja 48 1.1)

Who wishes to profit by inappropriate means
is tormented.
The Cetans who killed Vedabbha
all fell into ruin.
Constellations: a past life story (Ja 49 1.1)

Waiting for a constellation,
a fool lets the good pass them by.
The good is the constellation of the good;
for what do the stars matter?
The Simpleton: a past life story (Ja 50 1.1)

A sacrifice of simpletons by the thousand
was pledged by me.
Now I shall sacrifice
many an unrighteous man.
The Great Virtuous One: a past life story (Ja 51 1.1)

A man should have hope,
the astute should not be disillusioned.
Now I truly see myself—
as I wished, so I became.
A Short Tale of Janaka: a past life story (Ja 52 1.1)

A man should make an effort
the astute should not be disillusioned.
Now I truly see myself,
lifted from the water to the shore.
The Full Cups: a past life story (Ja 53 1.1)

The cups stay just as full,
while the ignorant talk goes on.
For this reason I know
this is not an excellent beer.
The What-fruit: a past life story (Ja 54 1.1)

This tree is not hard to climb,
nor is it far from the village.
For this reason I know
this tree is not sweet-fruited.
Prince Five-Weapons: a past life story (Ja 55 1.1)

He whose heart is not stuck,
a man of intrepid mind,
develops skillful qualities
for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.
Gradually he would attain
the ending of all fetters.
The Mass of Gold: a past life story (Ja 56 1.1)

He whose heart is well-forged,
a man of cheerful mind,
develops skillful qualities
for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.
Gradually he would attain
the ending of all fetters.
The Lord of Langurs: a past life story (Ja 57 1.1)

Whoever possesses these four qualities
like you, lord of langurs—
truth, principle, steadfastness, and generosity—
escapes the visible foe.
Three Qualities: a past life story (Ja 58 1.1)

Whoever possesses these three qualities
like you, lord of langurs—
adroitness, heroism, wisdom—
escapes the visible foe.
The Drummer: a past life story (Ja 59 1.1)

Blow, blow, don’t overblow,
for overblowing is bad.
By blowing a hundred was gained,
by overblowing it was lost.
The Horn-Blower: a past life story (Ja 60 1.1)

Blow, blow, don’t overblow,
for overblowing is bad.
By blowing riches were earned,
but your blowing dad blew it.
The Spell of the Unpleasant: a past life story (Ja 61 1.1)

The women in the world called unclaimed—
there is no confining them.
They are rude and full of desires,
like an all-consuming flame.
Leaving them behind, I shall go forth
and foster seclusion.
Since Infancy: a past life story (Ja 62 1.1)

The brahmin who played
the harp while blindfolded
had raised his wife since infancy—
who would ever trust such women?
The Philosopher: a past life story (Ja 63 1.1)

Hateful ingrates!
Slanderous traitors!
Live the spiritual life, mendicant,
you will not be bereft of happiness.
Hard to Understand: a past life story (Ja 64 1.1)

Do not rejoice, “She loves me,”
nor lament, “She loves me not.”
The mood of women is hard to understand,
like the track of fish in water.
Dissatisfaction: a past life story (Ja 65 1.1)

Just like rivers and roads,
taverns, hotels, and pubs,
are those called women in the world.
Sages do not get angry with them.
Queen Sweetheart: a past life story (Ja 66 1.1)

One wish I had in the past,
before I won Queen Sweetheart.
But when I won the moon-eyed lady,
wish upon wish was born.
In My Lap: a past life story (Ja 67 1.1)

A son in my lap, Your Majesty,
or a husband while walking the street—
but I don’t see the place
from where I can fetch a brother.
At Sāketa: a past life story (Ja 68 1.1)

In whom the mind settles,
and the heart too is confident—
gladly one would trust in
that man not seen before.
Vomited Poison: a past life story (Ja 69 1.1)

Curse that vomited poison,
which I vomited for the sake of life
and now shall consume again.
Death is better for me than life!
The Spade: a past life story (Ja 70 1.1)

That victory is not a good victory
which may be undone.
That victory is a good victory
which may not be undone.
The Warding Tree: a past life story (Ja 71 1.1)

Whoever wishes to do afterwards
tasks they should have done before,
like the one who broke a branch off the Warding Tree,
afterwards is tormented by regrets.
The Virtuous Elephant: a past life story (Ja 72 1.1)

An ungrateful person,
always looking for opportunity,
even if given the whole earth,
would still not be satisfied.
The Truth, It Seems: a past life story (Ja 73 1.1)

The truth, it seems, was spoken
by certain people here—
better a floating log
than a certain person.
The Law of Trees: a past life story (Ja 74 1.1)

It is well for the many relatives,
the trees born in the forest.
The wind sweeps off one standing alone,
even the enormous lord of the forest.
The Fish: a past life story (Ja 75 1.1)

Thunder forth, Pajjuna!
Disperse the trove of the crow!
Subject the crow to sorrow,
and free me from sorrow!
Unsuspecting: a past life story (Ja 76 1.1)

I am unsuspecting in the village;
in the wilderness there’s no peril for me:
I ride upon the straight path
with love and compassion.
Sixteen Great Dreams: a past life story (Ja 77 1.1)
Sixteen Great Dreams: a past life story (Ja 77 2.1)
Sixteen Great Dreams: a past life story (Ja 77 2.4)
No perversion of reality is happening here for me.
Herring, the Miser: a past life story (Ja 78 1.1)

Both are lame, both crippled,
both cross-eyed,
and both covered in warts:
I see not which is Herring.
The Harsh Sound: a past life story (Ja 79 1.1)

When cows were plundered and killed,
houses burned down, and people abducted,
then came the son of she whose son is dead,
sounding the harsh drum of war.
The Mark On the Sword: a past life story (Ja 126 1.1)

That is good for some,
ill for others.
Therefore not all is good,
nor is all ill.
The Peacock: a past life story (Ja 159 1.1)

This Clear-eyed One arises, the One King,
palomino-colored, shining over the earth.
I bow especially to you, palomino-colored, shining over the earth:
guarded by you let us live out this day.
The Peacock: a past life story (Ja 159 2.1)

Those brahmins who are knowledge-masters with respect to all things,
I worship them, may they keep me safe.
Hail the Awakened Ones, hail Awakening!
Homage to the freed ones, homage to freedom!
Having made this protection,
the peacock wanders seeking.
The Peacock: a past life story (Ja 159 3.1)

This Clear-eyed One sets, the One King,
palomino-colored, shining over the earth.
I bow especially to you, palomino-colored, shining over the earth:
guarded by you let us live out this night.
The Peacock: a past life story (Ja 159 4.1)

Those brahmins who are knowledge-masters with respect to all things,
I worship them, may they keep me safe.
Hail the Awakened Ones, hail Awakening!
Homage to the freed ones, homage to freedom!
Having made this protection,
the peacock made his home.
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 1.1)

“Those folk sow and reap,
men living on the fruit of their work.
They have no share of this island.
This is better far than India!”
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 2.1)

“When the fifteenth day full moon has risen,
there will be a great flood from the sea,
drowning this splendid isle.
Let it not destroy you all! Go to some other haven!”
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 3.1)

“Never shall a mighty flood of water from the sea
drown this splendid isle—
I have seen that through many a sign.
Don’t fear! Why worry? Celebrate!
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 4.1)

You’ve come to this splendid abode,
full of food and drink.
I see no danger for you at all.
Celebrate, even unto the sons of sons!”
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 5.1)

“This god in the southern quarter
crying, ‘It is safe!’: his is the truth!
The northern doesn’t know if there’s a danger or not.
Don’t fear! Why worry? Celebrate!”
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 6.1)

“As these spirits argue,
one reporting danger, one safety,
please heed my advice,
lest we perish swift and fleet.
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 7.1)

Let all join together to build a boat,
a strong vessel fully equipped.
If this southern one speaks true,
and is falsely rejected by the northern,
it shall serve us in time of need,
and we would not give up the island.
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 8.1)

But if the northern speaks true,
and is falsely rejected by the southern,
then having all boarded the boat,
we shall cross safely to the far shore.
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 9.1)

Truly, best not accept the last word that came your way,
when what was spoken by the first was best.
Who here accepts the truth after examination,
that man goes to the best place.”
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 10.1)

Just as, in the middle of the watery sea,
the merchants fled to safety by their own efforts,
so, realizing his future welfare,
he of vast wisdom transgresses not at all.
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 11.1)

Fools deluded by desire for tastes,
not realizing their future welfare,
sink down in face of present need,
like those people in mid-ocean.
The Sea Merchants: a past life story (Ja 466 12.1)

Prepare what must be done for the future, thinking,
“Let what must be done not harm me on the day the duty ripens.”
The kind who acts to prepare what must be done,
is not harmed by what must be done on the day the duty ripens.
Khuddaka Nikaya (Ja 534 23.2)
Bhāsvaravarṇa occurs at Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.14. There it describes a man’s soul purified by the fires of cremation. By this point in the Pali its use is more mundane.
The Three Refuges (Kp 1 1.1)
Homage to him, the blessed one, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha!
The Three Refuges (Kp 1 2.1)

I take refuge in the Buddha,
I take refuge in the Teaching,
I take refuge in the Saṅgha.
The Three Refuges (Kp 1 3.1)
The Three Refuges (Kp 1 4.1)
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 1.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from killing living creatures.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 2.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from stealing.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 3.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from sexual activity.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 4.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from lying.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 5.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 6.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from food at the wrong time.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 7.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from seeing shows of dancing, singing, and music.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 8.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from attiring and adorning myself with garlands, fragrance, and makeup.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 9.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from high and luxurious beds.
The Ten Precepts (Kp 2 10.1)
I undertake the precept to refrain from receiving gold and currency.
The Thirty-Two Parts of the Body (Kp 3 1.1)

“In this body there is head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, brain, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.”
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 1.1)
What is the one? All sentient beings are sustained by food.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 2.1)
What is the two? Name and form.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 3.1)
What is the three? Three feelings.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 4.1)
What is the four? Four noble truths.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 5.1)
What is the five? Five grasping aggregates.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 6.1)
What is the six? Six interior sense fields.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 7.1)
What is the seven? Seven awakening factors.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 8.1)
What is the eight? The noble eightfold path.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 9.1)
What is the nine? Nine abodes of sentient beings.
The Boy’s Questions (Kp 4 10.1)
What is the ten? One endowed with ten factors is called “perfected”.
Blessings (Kp 5 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. That deity addressed the Buddha in verse:
Blessings (Kp 5 2.1)

“Many gods and humans
have thought about blessings
desiring well-being:
declare the highest blessing.”
Blessings (Kp 5 3.1)

“Not to fraternize with fools,
but to fraternize with the wise,
and honoring those worthy of honor:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 4.1)

Living in a suitable region,
having made merit in the past,
being rightly resolved in oneself,
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 5.1)

Education and a craft,
discipline and training,
and well-spoken speech:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 6.1)

Caring for mother and father,
kindness to children and partners,
and unstressful work:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 7.1)

Giving and righteous conduct,
kindness to relatives,
blameless deeds:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 8.1)

Desisting and abstaining from evil,
avoiding drinking liquor,
diligence in good qualities:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 9.1)

Respect and placidity,
contentment and gratitude,
and timely listening to the teaching:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 10.1)

Patience, being easy to admonish,
the sight of ascetics,
and timely discussion of the teaching:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 11.1)

Fervor and chastity
seeing the noble truths,
and realization of extinguishment:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 12.1)

Though touched by worldly conditions,
their mind does not tremble;
sorrowless, stainless, secure:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Kp 5 13.1)

Having completed these things,
undefeated everywhere;
everywhere they go in safety:
this is their highest blessing.”
Gems (Kp 6 1.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky;
may beings all be of happy heart,
and listen carefully to what is said.
Gems (Kp 6 2.1)

So pay heed, all you beings,
have love for humankind,
who day and night bring offerings;
please protect them diligently.
Gems (Kp 6 3.1)

There’s no wealth this life or the next,
no sublime gem in the heavens,
that equals the Realized One.
This sublime gem is in the Buddha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 4.1)

Ending, dispassion, the undying, the sublime,
attained by the Sakyan Sage immersed in samādhi;
there is nothing equal to that Dhamma.
This sublime gem is in the Dhamma:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 5.1)

The purity praised by the highest Buddha,
is said to be the “immersion with immediate fruit”;
no equal to that immersion is found.
This sublime gem is in the Dhamma:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 6.1)

The eight individual persons praised by the good
are the four pairs of the Holy One’s disciples;
they are worthy of religious donations,
what’s given to them is very fruitful.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 7.1)

Dedicated to Gotama’s dispensation,
strong-minded, free of sense desire,
they’ve attained the goal, plunged into freedom from death,
and enjoy the quenching they’ve freely gained.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 8.1)

As Indra’s pillar rooted in earth
is not shaken by the four winds,
I say a true person is like this,
who sees the noble truths in experience.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 9.1)

Those who fathom the noble truths
taught by the one of deep wisdom,
do not take an eighth life,
even if they are hugely negligent.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 10.1)

When they attain to vision
they give up three things:
substantialist view, doubt, and any
attachment to precepts and observances.
Gems (Kp 6 11.1)

They’re freed from the four places of loss,
and cannot do six things.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 12.1)

Even if they do a bad deed
by body, speech, or mind,
they are unable to conceal it;
this, it’s said, is the inability of one who has seen the truth.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 13.1)

Like a tall forest tree crowned with flowers
in the first month of summer;
that’s how he taught the superb Dhamma,
leading to extinguishment, the ultimate benefit.
This sublime gem is in the Buddha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 14.1)

The superb, knower of the superb, giver of the superb, bringer of the superb;
taught the superb Dhamma supreme.
This sublime gem is in the Buddha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 15.1)

The old is ended, nothing new is produced;
their minds have no desire for future rebirth.
Withered are the seeds, there’s no desire for growth,
those attentive ones are extinguished like this lamp.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Kp 6 16.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
the Realized One is honored by gods and humans!
We bow to the Buddha! May you be safe!
Gems (Kp 6 17.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
the Realized One is honored by gods and humans!
We bow to the Dhamma! May you be safe!
Gems (Kp 6 18.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
the Realized One is honored by gods and humans!
We bow to the Saṅgha! May you be safe!
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 1.1)

Outside the walls they stand and wait,
at the junctions and the crossroads.
Returning to their former homes
they wait beside the door posts.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 2.1)

But when lavish food and drink
of many kinds is set out,
no one remembers them at all,
because of those beings’s deeds.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 3.1)

That’s why those who have compassion
give to their relatives
food and drink at the right time,
that’s clean, delicious, and suitable.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 4.1)

“May this be for our relatives!
May our relatives be happy!”
Those ghosts who have gathered there,
the departed relatives who have come
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 5.1)

for the lavish food and drink
gratefully express appreciation:
“May our relatives live long!
For those to whom we owe this gain,
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 6.1)

who have given honor to us,
it will not be fruitless for the donor.”
There is no farming there,
no cow pasture can be found;
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 7.1)

likewise there’s no trading,
and no commerce in gold coin.
The departed, the dead in that place
live on what is given here.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 8.1)

Just as water that rains on high
flows down to the plains,
so too what is given here
aids the departed ghosts.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 9.1)

Just as the rivers full
swell the ocean seas
so too what is given here
aids the departed ghosts.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 10.1)

Thinking: “They gave to me, they did for me,
they were my family, friend, comrade”,
give offerings to departed kin,
remembering past deeds.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 11.1)

For neither tears nor grief
or other lamentations
are of any use to the departed,
so long as their relatives stay like this.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 12.1)

This offering that has been given,
well placed in the Saṅgha,
is for their lasting welfare,
and aids them right away.
Outside the Walls (Kp 7 13.1)

The relative’s duty has now been shown:
how high honor to departed is performed,
how the mendicants can be kept strong,
and how no little merit is produced by you.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 1.1)

A person stores away their savings
in a deep trove by the water’s edge:
“When need arises
it will be there to help
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 2.1)

free me from rulers if I am slandered,
or from bandits if harassed,
or to release me from debt,
or in case of famine or losses.”
What the world calls savings
get stored away for such reasons.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 3.1)

But no matter how well stored away they are
in a deep pit by the water’s edge,
all their savings will fail
to aid them all the time.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 4.1)

For perhaps those savings shift from there,
or they forget what marks the site,
or dragons make off with them,
or spirits carry them away,
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 5.1)

or unloved heirs
secretly unearth them.
When their merit is used up,
all of that will vanish.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 6.1)

But by giving and morality,
restraint and self-control,
a woman or man
keeps their savings safe.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 7.1)

At a shrine or with the Saṅgha,
with mother or father,
or else an elder sibling,
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 8.1)

those savings are kept safe,
they stay with you, undecaying.
We must go on leaving all behind,
only this you take when you go.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 9.1)

You don’t have to share it with others,
no thief makes off with your savings.
An attentive one would make merit,
the savings that stay with you.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 10.1)

Such savings grant every desire
of gods and humans too.
Whatever it is that they wish for
through this they have it all.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 11.1)

Good looks, a sweet voice,
a good shape, and good appearance,
leadership and followers:
through this they have it all.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 12.1)

Sovereignty of a local kingdom,
the happiness of a Wheel-Turning Monarch,
even kingship in the heavens:
through this they have it all.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 13.1)

Human success,
heavenly delight,
attaining extinguishment:
through this they have it all.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 14.1)

Relying on having good friends,
rational application of effort,
mastery of knowledge and freedom:
through this they have it all.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 15.1)

Analytical knowledge, the liberations,
the perfections of the disciple,
the plane of an independent Buddha:
through this they have it all.
A Treasure Trove (Kp 8 16.1)

This accomplishment in merit
is so very beneficial.
That’s why the attentive and the astute
praise the making of merit.
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 1.1)

Those who are skilled in the meaning of scripture
should practice as follows to realize the state of peace.
Let them be capable and upright, very upright,
easy to speak to, gentle and humble;
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 2.1)

content and unburdensome,
unbusied, living lightly,
alert, with senses calmed,
courteous, not fawning on families.
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 3.1)

Let them not do the slightest thing
that others who are wise would blame.
May they be happy and safe!
May all beings be happy!
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 4.1)

Whatever living creatures there are
with not a one left out—
frail or firm, long or large,
medium, small, tiny or round,
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 5.1)

seen or unseen,
living far or near,
those who have been born and those about to be born—
may all beings be happy!
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 6.1)

Let none deceive another,
nor look down on anyone anywhere.
Though provoked or aggrieved,
let them not wish pain on each other.
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 7.1)

Even as a mother would protect with her life
her child, her only child,
so too for all creatures
unfold a boundless heart.
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 8.1)

With love for the whole world,
unfold a boundless heart:
above, below, all round,
unconstricted, without enmity or foe.
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 9.1)

When standing, walking, sitting,
or lying down while yet unweary,
keep this ever in mind;
for this, they say, is a divine meditation in this life.
The Discourse on Love (Kp 9 10.1)

Avoiding harmful views,
virtuous, accomplished in insight,
with desire for sensual pleasures dispelled,
they never return to a womb again.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 1.1)

When anger surges, they drive it out,
as with medicine a cobra’s spreading venom.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 2.1)

They’ve cut off greed entirely,
like a lotus plucked flower and stalk.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 3.1)

They’ve cut off craving entirely,
drying up that swift-flowing stream.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 4.1)

They’ve swept away conceit entirely,
as a fragile bridge of reeds by a great flood.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 5.1)

In future lives they find no worth,
as an inspector of fig trees finds no flower.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 6.1)

They hide no anger within,
passed beyond any kind of existence.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 7.1)

Their mental vibrations are cleared away,
internally clipped off entirely.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 8.1)

They have not run too far nor run back,
but have gone beyond all this proliferation.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 9.1)

They have not run too far nor run back,
for they know that nothing in the world is what it seems.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 10.1)

They have not run too far nor run back,
knowing nothing is what it seems, free of greed.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 11.1)

They have not run too far nor run back,
knowing nothing is what it seems, free of lust.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 12.1)

They have not run too far nor run back,
knowing nothing is what it seems, free of hate.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 13.1)

They have not run too far nor run back,
knowing nothing is what it seems, free of delusion.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 14.1)

They have no underlying tendencies at all,
and are rid of unskillful roots,
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 15.1)

They have nothing born of distress at all
to make them to return to the near shore.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 16.1)

No snarl grows in them at all,
that would shackle them to a new life.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Serpent (Snp 1.1 17.1)

They’ve given up the five hindrances,
untroubled, rid of indecision, free of thorns.
Such a mendicant sheds the near shore and the far,
as a serpent its old worn-out skin.
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 1.1)

“I’ve boiled my rice and drawn my milk,” said Dhaniya the rancher,
“I stay with my family along the bank of the Mahī.
My hut is roofed, my sacred fire kindled:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 2.1)

“I boil not with anger and have drawn out hard-heartedness,” said the Buddha,
“I stay for one night along the bank of the Mahī.
My hut is wide open, my fire is quenched:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 3.1)

“No gadflies or mosquitoes are found,” said Dhaniya,
“cows graze on the lush meadow grass.
They get by even when the rain comes:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 4.1)

“I bound a raft and prepared it well,” said the Buddha,
“and with it I crossed over, went to the far shore, and dispelled the flood.
Now I have no need for a raft:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 5.1)

“My wife is obedient, not wanton,” said Dhaniya,
“long have we lived together happily.
I hear nothing bad about her:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 6.1)

“My mind is obedient and freed,” said the Buddha,
“long nurtured and well-tamed.
Nothing bad is found in me:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 7.1)

“I am self-employed,” said Dhaniya,
“and my healthy children likewise.
I hear nothing bad about them:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 8.1)

“I am no one’s lackey,” said the Buddha,
“with what I have earned I wander the world.
I have no need for wages:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 9.1)

“I have heifers and sucklings,” said Dhaniya,
“cows in calf and breeding cows.
I’ve also got a bull, captain of the herd here:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 10.1)

“I have no heifers or sucklings,” said the Buddha,
“no cows in calf or breeding cows.
I haven’t got a bull, captain of the herd here:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 11.1)

“The stakes are driven in, unshakable,” said Dhaniya,
“The grass halters are new and well-woven,
not even the sucklings can break them:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 12.1)

“Like a bull I broke the bonds,” said the Buddha,
“like an elephant I snapped the vine.
I will never lie in a womb again:
so rain forth, heavens, if you wish.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 13.1)

Right then a vast cloud rained forth,
soaking the uplands and valleys.
Hearing the heavens rain down,
Dhaniya said this:
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 14.1)

“It is no small gain for us
that we have seen the Buddha.
We come to you for refuge, Clear-eyed One.
O great sage, please be our Teacher.
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 15.1)

My wife and I, obedient,
shall lead the spiritual life under the Holy One.
Gone beyond birth and death,
we shall make an end of suffering.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 16.1)

“Children bring you delight!” said Māra the Wicked,
“Cattle also bring you delight!
For attachments are a man’s delight;
without attachments there’s no delight.”
The Wealthy Rancher (Snp 1.2 17.1)

“Your children bring you sorrow,” said the Buddha,
“Your cattle also bring you sorrow.
For attachments are a man’s sorrow;
without attachments there are no sorrows.”
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 1.1)

When you’ve laid down violence toward all creatures,
not harming even a single one,
don’t wish for a child, let alone a companion:
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 2.1)

Those with close relationships have affection,
following which this pain arises.
Seeing this danger born of affection,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 3.1)

When feelings for friends and loved ones
are tied up in selfish love, you miss out on the goal.
Seeing this peril in intimacy,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 4.1)

As a spreading bamboo gets entangled,
so does concern for partners and children.
Like a bamboo shoot unobstructed,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 5.1)

As a wild deer loose in the forest
grazes wherever it wants,
a smart person looking for freedom would
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 6.1)

When among friends, whether staying in place
or going on a journey, you’re always on call.
Looking for the uncoveted freedom,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 7.1)

Among friends you have fun and games,
and for children you are full of fondness.
Though loathe to depart from those you hold dear,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 8.1)

At ease in any quarter, unresisting,
content with whatever comes your way;
prevailing over adversities, dauntless,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 9.1)

Even some renunciates are hard to please,
as are some layfolk dwelling at home.
Don’t worry about others’ children,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 10.1)

Having shed the marks of the home life,
like the fallen leaves of the Shady Orchid Tree;
having cut the bonds of the home life, a hero would
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 11.1)

If you find an alert companion,
an attentive friend to live happily together,
then, overcoming all adversities,
wander with them, joyful and mindful.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 12.1)

If you find no alert companion,
an attentive friend to live happily together,
then, like a king who flees his conquered realm,
wander alone like a tusker in the wilds.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 13.1)

Clearly we praise the blessing of a friend,
it’s good to be with friends your equal or better.
But failing to find them, eating blamelessly,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 14.1)

Though made of shining gold, well-finished by a smith,
when two bracelets share the same arm
they clash up against each other. Seeing this,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 15.1)

Thinking, “So too, if I had a partner,
there’d be flattery or curses.”
Seeing this peril in the future,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 16.1)

Sensual pleasures are diverse, sweet, delightful;
appearing in disguise they disturb the mind.
Seeing danger in sensual stimulations,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 17.1)

This is a calamity, a boil, a disaster,
an illness, a dart, and a danger for me.
Seeing this peril in sensuality,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 18.1)

Heat and cold, hunger and thirst,
wind and sun, flies and reptiles:
having put up with all these things,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 19.1)

As a full-grown elephant, lotus-fond, magnificent,
forsaking the herd,
stays as it pleases in the forest,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 20.1)

It’s impossible for one who delights in company
to experience even temporary freedom.
Heeding the speech of the Kinsman of the Sun,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 21.1)

Thinking, “I have left twisted views behind,
reached the sure way, and gained the path;
I’ve given rise to knowledge, and need no one to guide me”,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 22.1)

No greed, no guile, no thirst, no slur,
dross and delusion is smelted off;
free of hoping for anything in the world,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 23.1)

Avoid a wicked companion,
blind to the good, habitually immoral.
Don’t befriend the heedless and the hankering, but
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 24.1)

Spend time with the learned who have memorized the teachings,
an eloquent and uplifting friend.
When you understand the meanings and have dispelled doubt,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 25.1)

When you realize that worldly fun and games
and pleasure are inadequate, unconcerned with them,
as one unadorned, a speaker of truth,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 26.1)

Children, partner, father, mother,
wealth and grain and relatives:
having given up sensual pleasures to this extent,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 27.1)

“This is a chain. Here there’s hardly any happiness,
little gratification, and it’s full of drawbacks.
It’s a hook.” Knowing this, a thoughtful person would
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 28.1)

Having burst apart the fetters,
like a fish that tears the net and swims free,
or a fire not returning to ground it has burned,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 29.1)

Eyes downcast, not footloose,
senses guarded, mind protected,
not festering or burning with desire,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 30.1)

Having shed the marks of the home life,
like the fallen leaves of the Orchid Tree,
and gone forth in the ocher robe,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 31.1)

Not wanton, nor rousing greed for tastes,
providing for no other, wandering indiscriminately for alms,
not attached to this family or that,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 32.1)

When you’ve given up five mental obstacles,
and cast aside all corruptions,
and cut off affection and hate, being independent,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 33.1)

When you’ve put pleasure and pain behind you,
and former happiness and sadness,
and gained equanimity serene and pure,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 34.1)

With energy roused to reach the ultimate goal,
not sluggish in mind or lazy,
vigorous, strong and powerful,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 35.1)

Not neglecting retreat and absorption,
always living in line with the teaching,
comprehending the danger in rebirths,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 36.1)

One whose aim is the ending of craving—
diligent, clever, learned, mindful, resolute—
who has appraised the teaching and is assured, destined for awakening, should
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 37.1)

Like a lion not startled by sounds,
like wind not caught in a net,
like water not sticking to a lotus,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 38.1)

Like the fierce-fanged lion, king of beasts,
who wanders as conqueror and victor,
you should frequent remote lodgings, and
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 39.1)

In time, cultivate freedom through
love, compassion, rejoicing, and equanimity.
Not upset by anything in the world,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 40.1)

Having given up greed, hate, and delusion,
having burst apart the fetters,
unafraid at the end of life,
live alone like a horned rhino.
The Horned Rhino (Snp 1.3 41.1)

They befriend you and serve you for their own sake;
these days it’s hard to find friends lacking ulterior motive.
Impure folk cleverly profit themselves—
live alone like a horned rhino.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Magadhans in the Southern Hills near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa. Now at that time the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Farmer had harnessed around five hundred plows, it being the season for sowing. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to where Bhāradvāja the Farmer was working. Now at that time Bhāradvāja the Farmer was distributing food. Then the Buddha went to where the distribution was taking place and stood to one side.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 2.1)
Bhāradvāja the Farmer saw him standing for alms and said to him, “I plough and sow, ascetic, and then I eat. You too should plough and sow, then you may eat.”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 3.1)
“I too plough and sow, brahmin, and then I eat.” “I don’t see the worthy Gotama with a yoke or plow or plowshare or goad or oxen, yet he says: ‘I too plough and sow, brahmin, and then I eat.’”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 4.1)
Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer addressed the Buddha in verse:
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 5.1)

“You claim to be a farmer,
but I don’t see you farming.
Tell me your farming when asked,
so I can recognize your farming.”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 6.1)

“Faith is my seed, fervor my rain,
and wisdom is my yoke and plough.
Conscience is my draft-pole, mind my strap,
mindfulness my plowshare and goad.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 7.1)

Guarded in body and speech,
I restrict my intake of food.
I use truth as my scythe,
and gentleness is my release.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 8.1)

Energy is my harnessed beast,
transporting me to sanctuary from the yoke.
Without turning back, it goes
to where there is no sorrow.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 9.1)

That’s how to do the farming
that has freedom from death as its fruit.
When you finish this farming
you’re released from all suffering.”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 10.1)

Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer poured milk-rice in a large bronze cup and presented it to the Buddha: “May the worthy Gotama eat the milk-rice! The worthy one is a farmer. For the worthy Gotama does the farming that has freedom from death as its fruit.”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 11.1)

“Food enchanted by a verse isn’t fit for me to eat.
That’s not the principle of those who see, brahmin.
The Buddhas cast aside things enchanted with verses.
Since there is such a principle, brahmin, that’s how they live.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 12.1)

Serve with other food and drink
the consummate one, the great seer,
with defilements ended and remorse stilled.
For he is the field for the seeker of merit.”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 13.1)

“Then, worthy Gotama, to whom should I give the milk-rice?” “Brahmin, I don’t see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who can properly digest this milk-rice, except the Realized One or one of his disciples. Well then, brahmin, throw out the milk-rice where there is little that grows, or drop it into water that has no living creatures.”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 14.1)

So Bhāradvāja the Farmer dropped the milk-rice in water that had no living creatures. And when the milk-rice was placed in the water, it sizzled and hissed, steaming and fuming. Suppose there was an iron cauldron that had been heated all day. If you placed it in the water, it would sizzle and hiss, steaming and fuming. In the same way, when the milk-rice was placed in the water, it sizzled and hissed, steaming and fuming.
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 15.1)

Then Bhāradvāja the Farmer, shocked and awestruck, went up to the Buddha, bowed down with his head to the Buddha’s feet, and said, “Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha. May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama’s presence?”
With Bhāradvāja the Farmer (Snp 1.4 16.1)

And Bhāradvāja the Farmer received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence. Not long after his ordination, Venerable Bhāradvāja, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, soon realized the supreme culmination of the spiritual path in this very life. He lived having achieved with his own insight the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness. He understood: “Rebirth is ended; the spiritual journey has been completed; what had to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this place.” And Venerable Bhāradvāja became one of the perfected.
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 1.1)

“I ask the sage abounding in wisdom,” said Cunda the smith,
“the Buddha, master of the teaching, free of craving,
best of men, excellent charioteer, please tell me this:
how many ascetics are there in the world?”
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 2.1)

“There are four ascetics, not a fifth.” said the Buddha to Cunda,
“Being asked to bear witness, I will explain them to you:
the path-victor, the path-teacher,
the path-liver, and the path-wrecker.”
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 3.1)

“Who is a path-victor according to the Buddhas?” said Cunda the smith,
“and how is one an unequaled explainer of the path?
Tell me when asked about one who lives the path,
then declare the path-wrecker.”
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 4.1)

“Rid of indecision, free of thorns,
delighting in extinguishment, not fawning,
a guide for the world with its gods.
The Buddhas say one such is victor of the path.
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 5.1)

Knowing the ultimate as ultimate,
they explain and analyze the teaching right here.
That sage unstirred, with doubt cut off,
is the second mendicant, I say, the teacher of the path.
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 6.1)

Living restrained and mindful on the path
of the well-taught passage of teaching,
cultivating blameless states,
is the third mendicant, I say, the path-liver.
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 7.1)

Dressed like one true to their vows,
pushy, rude, a corrupter of families,
devious, unrestrained, chaff,
the path-wrecker’s life is a sham.
With Cunda (Snp 1.5 8.1)

A layperson who gets this,
a learned, wise noble disciple,
knows that ‘They are not all like that one’.
So when they see them they don’t lose their faith.
For how could one equate them—
the corrupt with the uncorrupt, the pure with the impure?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity addressed the Buddha in verse:
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 2.1)

“We ask Gotama
about a man’s downfall.
We have come to ask you, sir:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 3.1)

“It’s easy to understand success,
understanding downfall is just as easy.
One who loves the teaching succeeds,
but a hater of the teaching meets their downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 4.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the first downfall.
Tell us the second, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 5.1)

“The bad are dear to him,
he has no love for the good.
He believes the teaching of the bad;
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 6.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the second downfall.
Tell us the third, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 7.1)

“Fond of sleep, fond of company,
a man who does no work;
he’s lazy, marked by anger,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 8.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the third downfall.
Tell us the fourth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 9.1)

“Though able, he does not look after
his mother and father
when elderly, past their prime,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 10.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the fourth downfall.
Tell us the fifth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 11.1)

“He deceives with lies
ascetics and brahmins
and other supplicants,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 12.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the fifth downfall.
Tell us the sixth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 13.1)

“A man with plenty of wealth,
including gold coin and food,
eats delicacies alone,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 14.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the sixth downfall.
Tell us the seventh, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 15.1)

“Vain of birth, wealth,
and clan, a man
looks down on his own family,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 16.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the seventh downfall.
Tell us the eighth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 17.1)

“In womanizing, drinking,
and gambling, a man
wastes all that he has earned,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 18.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the eighth downfall.
Tell us the ninth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 19.1)

“Not content with his own partners,
he debauches himself with prostitutes,
and with others’ partners,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 20.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the ninth downfall.
Tell us the tenth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 21.1)

“A man well past his prime
marries a girl with budding breasts;
he cannot sleep for jealousy,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 22.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the tenth downfall.
Tell us the eleventh, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 23.1)

“He places in authority
a woman or a man
who’s a drunkard and a wastrel,
and that leads to his downfall.”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 24.1)

“We understand what you’re saying,
this is the eleventh downfall.
Tell us the twelfth, Blessed One:
what leads to downfall?”
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 25.1)

“A man of little wealth and strong craving,
born into an aristocratic family,
sets his sights on kingship,
and that leads to his downfall.
Downfalls (Snp 1.6 26.1)

Seeing these downfalls in the world,
an astute and noble person,
accomplished in vision,
will enjoy a world of grace.”
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Now at that time in the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper’s home the sacred flame had been kindled and the oblation prepared. Wandering indiscriminately for almsfood in Sāvatthī, the Buddha approached Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper’s house.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 2.1)
Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper saw the Buddha coming off in the distance and said to him, “Stop right there, shaveling! Right there, fake ascetic! Right there, lowlife!”
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 3.1)

When he said this, the Buddha said to him, “But brahmin, do you know what is a lowlife or what are the qualities that make you a lowlife?” “No I do not, worthy Gotama. Please, worthy Gotama, teach me this matter so I can understand what is a lowlife or what are the qualities that make you a lowlife.” “Well then, brahmin, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.” “Yes, worthy sir,” Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper replied. The Buddha said this:
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 4.1)

“Irritable and acrimonious,
wicked and offensive,
a man deficient in view, deceitful:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 5.1)

He harms living creatures
born of womb or of egg,
and has no kindness for creatures:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 6.1)

He destroys and devastates
villages and towns,
a notorious oppressor:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 7.1)

Whether in village or wilderness,
he steals what belongs to others,
taking what has not been given:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 8.1)

Having fallen into debt,
when pressed to pay up he flees, saying
‘I don’t owe you anything!’:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 9.1)

Wanting some item or other,
he attacks a person in the street
and takes it:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 10.1)

For his own sake or the sake of another,
or for the sake of wealth, a man
tells a lie when asked to bear witness:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 11.1)

He is spied among the partners
of relatives and friends,
by force or seduction:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 12.1)

Though able, he does not look after
his mother and father
when elderly, past their prime:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 13.1)

He hits or verbally abuses
his mother or father,
brother, sister, or mother-in-law:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 14.1)

When asked about the good,
he teaches what is bad,
giving secretive advice:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 15.1)

Having done a bad deed, he wishes,
‘May no one find me out!’
His deeds are underhand:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 16.1)

When visiting another family
he eats their delicious food,
but does not return the honor:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 17.1)

He deceives with lies
ascetics and brahmins
and other supplicants:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 18.1)

When time comes to offer a meal
to brahmins or ascetics,
he abuses them and does not give:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 19.1)

He talks about what never happened,
being wrapped up in delusion,
chasing after some item or other:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 20.1)

He extols himself
and disparages others,
brought down by his pride:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 21.1)

He’s a bully and a miser,
of corrupt wishes, stingy, and devious,
shameless, imprudent:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 22.1)

He insults the Buddha
or his disciple,
whether lay or renunciate:
know him as a lowlife.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 23.1)

He claims to be a perfected one,
when he really is no such thing.
In the world with its divinities,
that crook is truly the lowest lowlife.
These who are called lowlifes
I have revealed to you.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 24.1)

You’re not a lowlife by birth,
nor by birth are you a brahmin.
You’re a lowlife by your deeds,
by deeds you’re a brahmin.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 25.1)

And also you should know
according to this example.
A corpse-worker’s son of the dog-eating caste
became renowned as Mātaṅga.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 26.1)

Mātaṅga achieved the highest fame
so very hard to find.
Lots of aristocrats and brahmins
came to serve him.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 27.1)

He ascended the stainless highway
that leads to the heavens;
having discarded sensual desire,
he was reborn in a realm of divinity.
His birth did not prevent him
from rebirth in the realm of divinity.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 28.1)

Those born in a brahmin family
who recite as kinsmen of the hymns,
are often discovered
in the midst of wicked deeds.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 29.1)

Blameworthy in this very life,
and in lives to come, a bad destination.
Their birth does not prevent them
from blame or bad destiny.
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 30.1)

You’re not a lowlife by birth,
nor by birth are you a brahmin.
You’re a lowlife by your deeds,
by deeds you’re a brahmin.”
The Lowlife (Snp 1.7 31.1)

When he had spoken, the brahmin Bhāradvāja the Fire-Worshiper said to the Buddha, “Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 1.1)

Those who are skilled in the meaning of scripture
should practice as follows to realize the state of peace.
Let them be capable and upright, very upright,
easy to speak to, gentle and humble;
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 2.1)

content and unburdensome,
unbusied, living lightly,
alert, with senses calmed,
courteous, not fawning on families.
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 3.1)

Let them not do the slightest thing
that others who are wise would blame.
May they be happy and safe!
May all beings be happy!
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 4.1)

Whatever living creatures there are
with not a one left out—
frail or firm, long or large,
medium, small, tiny or round,
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 5.1)

seen or unseen,
living far or near,
those who have been born and those about to be born—
may all beings be happy!
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 6.1)

Let none deceive another,
nor look down on anyone anywhere.
Though provoked or aggrieved,
let them not wish pain on each other.
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 7.1)

Even as a mother would protect with her life
her child, her only child,
so too for all creatures
unfold a boundless heart.
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 8.1)

With love for the whole world,
unfold a boundless heart:
above, below, all round,
unconstricted, without enmity or foe.
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 9.1)

When standing, walking, sitting,
or lying down while yet unweary,
keep this ever in mind;
for this, they say, is a divine meditation in this life.
The Discourse on Love (Snp 1.8 10.1)

Avoiding harmful views,
virtuous, accomplished in insight,
with desire for sensual pleasures dispelled,
they never return to a womb again.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 1.1)

“Today is the fifteenth day sabbath,” said Sātāgira, the native spirit of mount Sātā,
“a holy night is at hand.
Come now, let us see Gotama,
the Teacher of peerless name.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 2.1)

“Isn’t his mind well-disposed,” said Hemavata, the native spirit of the Himalayas,
“impartial toward all creatures?
And aren’t his thoughts under control
when it comes to likes and dislikes?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 3.1)

“His mind is well-disposed,” said Sātāgira,
“impartial toward all creatures.
His thoughts are under control
when it comes to his likes and dislikes.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 4.1)

“Doesn’t he not steal?” said Hemavata,
“And doesn’t he harm not a creature?
Isn’t he far from negligence?
And doesn’t he not neglect absorption?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 5.1)

“He does not take what is not given,” said Sātāgira,
“and he harms not a creature.
He is far from negligence—
the Buddha does not neglect absorption.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 6.1)

“Doesn’t he avoid lying?” said Hemavata,
“And doesn’t he not speak sharply?
Doesn’t he avoid backbiting,
as well as speaking nonsense?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 7.1)

“He does not lie,” said Sātāgira,
“nor does he speak sharply.
He avoids backbiting,
and thoughtfully speaks wise counsel.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 8.1)

“Doesn’t he find sensual pleasures unattractive?” said Hemavata,
“And isn’t his mind unclouded?
Hasn’t he escaped delusion?
Does his eye see clearly in all things?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 9.1)

“He does not find sensual pleasures attractive,” said Sātāgira,
“and his mind is unclouded.
He has escaped all delusion—
the Buddha, whose eye sees clearly in all things.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 10.1)

“Isn’t he accomplished in knowledge?” said Hemavata,
“And doesn’t he live a pure life?
Aren’t his defilements all ended?
Doesn’t he have no future lives?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 11.1)

“He is accomplished in knowledge,” said Sātāgira,
“and he does live a pure life.
His defilements are all ended,
there’ll be no more future lives for him.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 12.1)

“Accomplished is the sage’s mind
in action and in speech,
and he’s accomplished in knowledge and conduct
as per the teaching you praise.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 13.1)

“Accomplished is the sage’s mind
in action and in speech,
and he’s accomplished in knowledge and conduct
as per the teaching you rejoice in.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 14.1)

Accomplished is the sage’s mind
in action and in speech,
and he’s accomplished in knowledge and conduct:
come now, let us see Gotama.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 15.1)

“The hero so lean, with antelope calves,
not greedy, eating little,
the sage meditating alone in the forest,
come now, let us see Gotama.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 16.1)

A giant, wandering alone like a lion,
unconcerned for sensual pleasures,
let’s approach him and ask about
release from the snare of death.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 17.1)

“The communicator, the instructor,
who has gone beyond all things,
Awakened, beyond enmities and fears,
let us ask Gotama.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 18.1)

“What has the world arisen in?” said Hemavata,
“What does it get close to?
By grasping what
is the world troubled in what?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 19.1)

“The world’s arisen in six,” said the Buddha to Hemavata.
“It gets close to six.
Derived from the six,
the world’s troubled in six.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 20.1)

“What is that grasping
by which the world is troubled?
Tell us the exit when asked:
how is one released from all suffering?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 21.1)

“The world has five kinds of sensual stimulation,
and the mind is said to be the sixth.
When you’ve discarded desire for these,
you’re released from all suffering.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 22.1)

This is the exit from the world,
explained in accord with the truth.
The way I’ve explained it is how
you’re released from all suffering.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 23.1)

“Who here crosses the flood,
Who crosses the deluge?
Who, not standing and unsupported,
does not sink in the deep?”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 24.1)

“Someone who is always endowed with ethics,
wise and serene,
inwardly reflective, mindful,
crosses the flood so hard to cross.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 25.1)

Someone who desists from sensual perception,
who has escaped all fetters,
and has ended relish for rebirth,
does not sink in the deep.”
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 26.1)

“Behold him of wisdom deep who sees the subtle meaning,
who has nothing, unattached to sensual life,
everywhere free,
the great seer treading the holy road.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 27.1)

Behold him of peerless name who sees the subtle meaning,
giver of wisdom, unattached to the realm of sensuality:
the all-knower, so very intelligent,
the great seer treading the noble road.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 28.1)

It was a fine sight for us today,
a good sunup, a good rising,
to see the Awakened One,
the undefiled one who has crossed the flood.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 29.1)

These thousand native spirits
powerful and glorious,
all go to you for refuge,
you are our supreme Teacher.
With Hemavata (Snp 1.9 30.1)

We shall journey
village to village, peak to peak,
paying homage to the Buddha,
and the clear rightness of the teaching!”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī in the haunt of the native spirit Āḷavaka. Then the native spirit Āḷavaka went up to the Buddha, and said to him: “Get out, ascetic!” Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went out. “Get in, ascetic!” Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went in.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 2.1)

For a second time … And for a third time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha, “Get out, ascetic!” Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went out. “Get in, ascetic!” Saying, “All right, respectable sir,” the Buddha went in.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 3.1)
And for a fourth time the native spirit Āḷavaka said to the Buddha, “Get out, ascetic!” “No, respectable sir, I won’t get out. Do what you must.”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 4.1)
“I will ask you a question, ascetic. If you don’t answer me, I’ll drive you insane, or explode your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you to the far shore of the Ganges!”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 5.1)

“I don’t see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans who could do that to me. But anyway, ask what you wish.” Then the native spirit Āḷavaka addressed the Buddha in verse:
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 6.1)

“What’s a person’s best wealth?
What brings happiness when practiced well?
What’s the sweetest taste of all?
The one they say has the best life: how do they live?”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 7.1)

“Faith here is a person’s best wealth.
The teaching brings happiness when practiced well.
Truth is the sweetest taste of all.
The one they say has the best life lives by wisdom.”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 8.1)

“How do you cross the flood?
How do you cross the deluge?
How do you get over suffering?
How do you get purified?”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 9.1)

“By faith you cross the flood,
and by diligence the deluge.
By energy you get past suffering,
and you’re purified by wisdom.”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 10.1)

“How do you get wisdom?
How do you earn wealth?
How do you get a good reputation?
How do you hold on to friends?
How do the departed not grieve
when passing from this world to the next?”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 11.1)

“One who is diligent and discerning
gains wisdom by wanting to learn,
having faith in the perfected ones,
and the teaching for becoming extinguished.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 12.1)

Being responsible, acting appropriately,
and working hard you earn wealth.
Truthfulness wins you a good reputation.
You hold on to friends by giving.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 13.1)

A faithful householder of discernment
who possesses these four qualities
does not grieve after passing away:
truth, principle, steadfastness, and generosity.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 14.1)

Go ahead, ask others as well,
there are many ascetics and brahmins.
See whether anything better is found
than truth, principle, generosity, and patience.”
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 15.1)

“Why now would I question
the many ascetics and brahmins?
Today I understand
what’s good for lives to come.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 16.1)

It was truly for my benefit
that the Buddha came to stay at Āḷavī.
Today I understand
where a gift is very fruitful.
With Āḷavaka (Snp 1.10 17.1)

I myself will journey
village to village, town to town,
paying homage to the Buddha,
and the clear rightness of the teaching!”
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 1.1)

Walking and standing,
sitting and lying down,
extending and contracting the limbs:
these are the movements of the body.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 2.1)

Linked together by bones and sinews,
plastered over with flesh and hide,
and covered by the skin,
the body is not seen as it is.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 3.1)

It’s full of guts and belly,
liver and bladder,
heart and lungs,
kidney and spleen,
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 4.1)

spit and snot,
sweat and fat,
blood and synovial fluid,
bile and grease.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 5.1)

Then in nine streams
the filth is always flowing.
There is muck from the eyes,
wax from the ears,
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 6.1)

and snot from the nostrils.
The mouth sometimes vomits
bile and sometimes phlegm.
And from the body, sweat and waste.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 7.1)

Then there is the hollow head
all filled with brains.
Governed by ignorance,
the fool thinks it’s lovely.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 8.1)

And when it lies dead,
bloated and livid,
dumped in a charnel ground,
the relatives forget it.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 9.1)

It’s devoured by dogs,
by jackals, wolves, and worms.
It’s devoured by crows and vultures,
and any other creatures there.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 10.1)

A wise mendicant here,
having heard the Buddha’s words,
fully understands it,
for they see it as it is.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 11.1)

“As this is, so is that,
as that is, so is this.”
They’d blanch desire for the body
inside and out.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 12.1)

That wise mendicant here
rid of desire and lust,
has found the peace free of death,
extinguishment, the state that does not pass.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 13.1)

This two-legged body is dirty and stinking,
full of different carcasses,
and oozing all over the place—
but still it is cherished!
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 14.1)

And if, on account of such a body,
someone prides themselves
or looks down on others—
what is that but a failure to see?
The Sage (Snp 1.12 1.1)

Peril stems from intimacy,
dust comes from an abode.
Freedom from abode and intimacy:
that is the sage’s vision.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 2.1)

Having cut down what’s grown, they wouldn’t replant,
nor would they nurture what’s growing.
That’s who they call a sage wandering alone,
the great seer has seen the state of peace.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 3.1)

Having appraised the fields and measured the seeds,
they wouldn’t nurture them with moisture.
Truly that sage who sees the ending of rebirth
has left speculation behind and is beyond reckoning.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 4.1)

Understanding all the planes of rebirth,
not wanting a single one of them;
truly that sage freed of greed
need not swim, for they have reached the far shore.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 5.1)

The vanquisher of all, knower of all, so very intelligent,
unsullied in the midst of all things,
has given up all, freed in the ending of craving:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 6.1)

Strong in wisdom, with precepts and observances intact,
serene, loving absorption, mindful,
released from chains, kind, undefiled:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 7.1)

The diligent sage wandering alone,
is unshaken by blame and praise—
like a lion not startled by sounds,
like wind not caught in a net,
like water not sticking to a lotus.
Leader of others, not by others led:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 8.1)

Steady as a post in a bathing-place
when others speak endlessly against them,
freed of greed, with senses stilled:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 9.1)

Steadfast, straight as a spindle,
horrified by wicked deeds,
discerning the just and the unjust:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 10.1)

Restrained, they do no evil,
young or middle-aged, the sage is self-controlled.
Irreproachable, he does not insult anyone:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 11.1)

When one who lives on charity receives alms,
from the top, the middle, or the leftovers,
they think it unworthy to praise or put down:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 12.1)

The sage lives refraining from sex,
even when young is not tied down,
refraining from indulgence and negligence, freed:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 13.1)

Understanding the world, the seer of the ultimate goal,
the unaffected one, having crossed the flood and the ocean,
has cut the ties, unattached and undefiled:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 14.1)

The two are not the same, far apart in lifestyle and conduct—
the householder providing for a wife, and the selfless one true to their vows.
The unrestrained householder kills other creatures,
while the restrained sage always protects living creatures.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 15.1)

As the crested blue-necked peacock flying through the sky
never approaches the speed of the swan,
so the householder cannot compete with the mendicant,
the sage meditating secluded in the woods.
Gems (Snp 2.1 1.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
may beings all be of happy heart,
and listen carefully to what is said.
